what_its_for: Tizanidine is a muscle relaxer used to treat muscle spasms and tightness (spasticity). It is often used for conditions like multiple sclerosis or spinal cord injuries that cause muscles to tighten or cramp.
how_to_take: Take tizanidine exactly as your doctor tells you. You can take it with or without food, but try to take it the same way each time — either always with food or always without food. Swallow the tablet or capsule whole. Do not crush, chew, or break it unless your doctor says it is okay. Do not suddenly stop taking this medicine without talking to your doctor first, as stopping too quickly can cause withdrawal symptoms like high blood pressure, fast heart rate, and shakiness.
dosing: The usual starting dose is 2 mg taken by mouth every 6 to 8 hours as needed for muscle spasms. Your doctor may slowly increase your dose based on how you respond. Do not take more than 3 doses in a 24-hour period. The maximum dose is 36 mg per day. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember — but only if it is not too close to the time of your next scheduled dose. If it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Never take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store tizanidine at room temperature, between 59°F and 86°F (15°C to 30°C). Keep it away from heat, direct light, and moisture. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep this medicine out of reach of children and pets. Do not flush unused medicine down the toilet — ask your pharmacist about the best way to safely throw it away.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking alcohol while taking tizanidine — it can increase drowsiness and dizziness and raise the risk of serious side effects. Do not drive, operate heavy machinery, or do any activity that requires you to be alert until you know how this medicine affects you. Avoid taking other medicines that make you sleepy (such as sleeping pills, anxiety medicines, or other muscle relaxers) unless your doctor approves. Avoid taking fluvoxamine (Luvox) or ciprofloxacin (Cipro) with tizanidine, as these combinations are dangerous. Avoid getting up too quickly from a sitting or lying position, as tizanidine can cause low blood pressure and dizziness.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away if you experience: severe dizziness or fainting, yellowing of the skin or eyes (signs of liver problems), nausea, stomach pain, unusual tiredness, dark-colored urine, hallucinations or confusion, a very slow or irregular heartbeat, or signs of an allergic reaction such as rash, itching, swelling of the face or throat, or trouble breathing. Also contact your doctor if your muscle spasms do not improve or get worse.
when_it_works: Tizanidine usually starts to work within 1 to 2 hours after you take a dose. It is a short-acting medicine, meaning its effects typically last about 3 to 6 hours. It is generally used for relief during specific times of the day when muscle tightness is most bothersome, not necessarily around the clock.
special_populations: Older adults: Tizanidine should be used with extra caution in older adults because it can cause more dizziness and a greater risk of falls. Doctors often start with a lower dose. Kidney problems: If you have kidney disease, your doctor may prescribe a lower dose and monitor you more closely. Liver problems: Tizanidine is broken down by the liver. It should be used carefully — or avoided — in people with liver disease. Your doctor may check your liver function with blood tests. Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Tell your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. The safety of tizanidine during pregnancy and breastfeeding has not been fully established. Children: Tizanidine is not approved for use in children, though doctors may sometimes prescribe it off-label. Always follow your doctor's specific guidance.
